button-name.whatItMeans: There's a submit button that only shows an arrow icon, and that icon is hidden from assistive technology, so the button has no text at all.
button-name.whoItAffects: Someone using a screen reader tabs to this button and hears only 'button' with no indication of what it does, so they can't confidently submit the form.
button-name.howToFix: Add a visually hidden text label inside the button (like 'Submit') or an aria-label="Submit" attribute on the <button> itself.

image-alt.whatItMeans: An image on the page has no text description, so anyone who can't see it has no idea what it is or why it's there.
image-alt.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear nothing useful (or just the filename) when they reach this image, losing any information or context it was meant to convey.
image-alt.howToFix: Add an alt attribute describing the image's purpose, or if it's purely decorative, set alt="" so screen readers skip it.

label.whatItMeans: An email input field on a form has no associated label text telling users what to type into it.
label.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear only 'edit text' with no clue it's for an email address, and voice-control users can't say a name to jump to the field.
label.howToFix: Add a <label for="..."> element tied to the input's id (or wrap the input in a <label>) with text like 'Email address'.

select-name.whatItMeans: A dropdown menu for choosing a plan (Free/Pro) has no name announced to assistive technology.
select-name.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear just 'combo box' with no idea it's the plan selector, making it confusing to choose an option.
select-name.howToFix: Add a <label> element linked to the select's id, or an aria-label="Choose plan" attribute on the <select>.

color-contrast.whatItMeans: Some text (a faint terms notice, a banner about a sale, and a faint 'all sales final' note) is too light or low-contrast against its background, making it hard to read.
color-contrast.whoItAffects: People with low vision, color blindness, or anyone reading on a bright screen or in glare will struggle to make out this text.
color-contrast.howToFix: Darken the text color or lighten/darken the background so the contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1 for normal text, per WCAG guidelines.

document-title.whatItMeans: The page has no <title> element, so it has no name shown in the browser tab or search results.
document-title.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear nothing when the page loads to confirm what page they're on, and everyone loses a way to identify the tab or bookmark it meaningfully.
document-title.howToFix: Add a descriptive <title> tag inside the <head> of the page, e.g. <title>Pricing – Company Name</title>.

html-has-lang.whatItMeans: The page's HTML doesn't declare what language it's written in.
html-has-lang.whoItAffects: Screen reader users may hear the page read aloud with the wrong pronunciation or accent because the software doesn't know the language.
html-has-lang.howToFix: Add a lang attribute to the opening <html> tag, e.g. <html lang="en"> for English.

link-name.whatItMeans: A link to the pricing page has no visible text or label — it's essentially an empty link.
link-name.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear 'link' with no description of where it goes, and can't tell it leads to pricing information.
link-name.howToFix: Add descriptive text inside the <a> tag, such as 'View pricing', or add an aria-label="View pricing" if the link uses only an icon.
